growth_story.headline: Offshore oil, pumped since 2019, turned Guyana's stop-start growth into a boom: income per person grew 23.0 percent a year over the last decade.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Guyana fell through the 1980s, then recovered fast, growing 5.7 percent a year in 1990–1997 as the country moved from a planned economy to a market one. From 1998 to 2005 growth nearly stopped, at 0.3 percent a year, as trade shocks, bad weather, political tension, a poor investment climate and the loss of skilled people weighed, and in 2005 severe floods and the closure of the largest gold mine hit at once. Growth picked up to 3.7 percent a year in 2006–2017, carried by high world prices for minerals and new mining, though mining created few jobs. Then came oil: found offshore in 2015 and first pumped in 2019, it lifted growth to 28.0 percent a year in 2018–2025, with 43.5 percent in 2020 alone. Over the last decade income per person grew 23.0 percent a year, against 3.9 in the decade before, and in 2025 it reached its highest level yet.

threads.title: Offshore oil arrives
threads.text: Oil was found off the coast in 2015 and first pumped in 2019. It has driven the fastest growth in the record: income per person rose 43.5 percent in 2020, 62.1 in 2022 and 18.6 in 2025, reaching a new peak in 2025.

threads.text: The government is using oil money to close gaps in infrastructure and in people's skills and health, and the economy outside oil has grown fast as well. The World Bank notes that this spending also adds to price pressure and to budget deficits.

threads.text: The IMF and the World Bank both list shortages of workers among the risks of growth this fast, with wages that could rise quickly. The World Bank adds that a stronger real exchange rate could make Guyana's other exports harder to sell.

threads.title: Market reforms, then stalling
threads.text: The move from a planned to a market economy brought quick growth in the early 1990s, but from 1998 growth stalled. Trade shocks, bad weather and political tension hurt farming and mining, while a poor investment climate and the departure of skilled people held growth down. In 2005 severe floods and the closure of the largest gold mine added to the losses.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person at a record in 2025, but that measure counts output, not what households keep. The World Bank reports large payments for services and income flowing out of the country in early 2026, and the IMF noted in 2025 that the last household survey was in 2019, so there is little recent data on poverty. The IMF's October 2026 release also gives a preliminary 2025 population well above the figure these data divide by, and fuller census results are still to come. If the higher figure holds, income per person is lower than the data show.
